conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Carter, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional health of new mothers. First, let me say: adjusting to life with a baby can be joyful and exhausting all at once; whatever you’re feeling right now is valid and worth listening to.

To help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’d like to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are no right or wrong responses; we just want to make sure we’re giving you the best support possible.

We’ll take it one question at a time. When you’re ready, we can begin.

**Question 1**  
Looking back over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly… it’s been really hard to laugh. My husband tried to joke with me yesterday about diaper explosions and, even though I could tell it was supposed to be funny, it just felt flat. I gave a little smile so he wouldn’t worry, but nothing felt truly funny inside.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No… that’s not how it’s felt for me. I don’t think I’ve really laughed at anything all week. Even when my partner or my mom tries to joke, it’s like I can’t feel it. I just feel… numb or heavy, like the laughter can’t reach me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it’s like nothing sounds worth the effort. I’ll think “that might be nice,” but the feeling fades before I can actually want to do it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for hours and I kept thinking it must be because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m not holding him the “correct” way or my milk isn’t “good” enough. Even when my partner says the baby’s just having a rough day, I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing—even though I can see her chest moving. Or I’ll lie awake picturing her crib tipping over or the diaper rash turning into some awful infection. I know it sounds extreme, but in the moment I can’t talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… sometimes it hits out of nowhere. I’ll just be folding the laundry and suddenly feel like something awful is about to happen—like a tight pressure in my chest and I can’t catch my breath. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening, and I’m left shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles, the laundry pile, the texts I haven’t answered, and I feel like I’m drowning. Some mornings I just sit on the couch while the baby naps, staring at the mess, too overwhelmed to start anything. I usually push through, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… a few nights this week I’d finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind just wouldn’t stop. I keep replaying everything I think I did wrong—did I burp him long enough, did I snap at my toddler, am I already ruining both kids? By the time the thoughts settle, it’s nearly time for the next feeding, so I lie there listening for every tiny sound he makes. I’m exhausted but sleep won’t come.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. It’s like this gray cloud follows me around. I’ll be changing her diaper and suddenly feel tears in my eyes for no clear reason. Everything just feels heavy and joyless. I keep waiting to “snap out of it,” but the sadness keeps creeping back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Once was in the grocery-store parking lot—he’d been screaming the whole drive, and when I finally got him quiet and went to grab the diaper bag, the strap snapped and everything spilled onto the asphalt. I just sat there crying in the front seat, feeling like I can’t even manage a simple errand. Another night it was while I rocked him at 3 a.m.—no real trigger, just overwhelming sadness that wouldn’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I feel down and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to end things. My babies need me, and even on the worst days that keeps me going.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wk post-delivery (perinatal context confirmed)  
Date: ___  
Clinician: ___  

I. Patient-Reported Symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety, panic spells, intrusive catastrophic thoughts about infant safety (Q4, Q5)  
- Overwhelm, difficulty coping with daily tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)  
- No self-harm ideation (Q10 denies)  

II. Pattern / Cluster  
Symptoms consistent with moderate-to-severe depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; onset post-delivery. Functional impairment evident (household tasks, sleep, social withdrawal).  

III. Screening Significance  
High index of suspicion for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and comorbid Anxiety Disorder. Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) recommended for quantification; assess for obsessive/intrusive thoughts of infant harm (common in perinatal anxiety).  

IV. Risk Factors Identified  
- Perinatal period (≤12 wk)  
- Persistent sadness, anhedonia, crying spells  
- Sleep disruption linked to rumination  
- Heightened anxiety/panic, catastrophic cognitions focused on infant  
- Feelings of maternal inadequacy, guilt  

V. Safety Note  
Patient explicitly denies suicidal or self-harm thoughts; no current safety concern reported. Continue routine safety inquiry at each contact.  

VI. Next Steps (screening level)  
Arrange formal EPDS; consider referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation and possible evidence-based psychotherapy ± medication consult.
